court: Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: Neighboring property owners bound by a restrictive covenant limiting use to 'a private dwelling house' sued to enjoin defendants from running their home as a tourist house, renting rooms to the traveling public by the day or longer. The court held that renting rooms to transient guests for hire is not use as 'a private dwelling,' is instead akin to a hotel or public boarding house, and enjoined the practice notwithstanding some change in neighborhood character and toleration of a few other similar violations nearby.

quotes.text: Beginning in November 1940, defendants have conducted a tourist house on their premises, without altering the structure of the building thereon, and pursuant thereto have rented rooms to strangers by the day or for any longer period desired.

An invitation to the general traveling public to the facilities of the home for hire certainly deprives a residence of its designation as a ‘private residence’. It comes closer to being a hotel or public boarding house, both held by the Taylor ease to be in violation of such a restriction.

Joseph K. Crager and Mary E. Crager are hereby enjoined from conducting their premises, 5934 Roosevelt Boulevard, Philadelphia, Pa., as a tourist house and from using said premises for any purpose other than as a private dwelling.

court: Erie County Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: Reviewing a borough ordinance requiring a license fee to keep inhabited house trailers on land, the court upheld the license as applied to landowners who rent space to trailers for profit as a commercial trailer camp, reasoning the camps impose extraordinary demands on police, fire, sanitation and other municipal services that justify a licensing fee under the police power. But the court struck the ordinance down as applied to a landowner who lived in his own trailer on his own land, holding that the right to occupy one's own home cannot be licensed absent a commercial use of the kind found in a boarding or rooming house.

quotes.text: Unquestionably, the right to have a home can be licensed only where conditions prevail which take the home out of the ordinary category, as for example where it is used for such commercial enterprise as a boarding or rooming house.
The right to live in a home is not a privilege which is subject to license; it is a human right.
But we see no constitutional objection to enforcement of this ordinance as a police measure against those who operate trailer camps for profit.
The effect of this ordinance as to appellant George is that the borough is licensing his right to establish his own home on his own land.

notes: Case concerns a municipal trailer-camp licensing ordinance, not a landlord-tenant lease/license/lodging classification, so characterization is left null; the boarding/rooming-house analogy is doctrinally on point for the police-power licensing question and is captured in doctrinal_concepts.
